prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A coarse-grained computational procedure based on the Finite Element Method is proposed to calculate the normal modes and mechanical response of proteins and their supramolecular assemblies. Motivated by the elastic network model, proteins are modeled as homogeneous isotropic elastic solids with volume defined by their solvent-excluded surface. The discretized Finite Element representation is obtained using a surface simplification algorithm that facilitates the generation of models of arbitrary prescribed spatial resolution. The procedure is applied to compute the normal modes of a mutant of T4 phage lysozyme and of filamentous actin, as well as the critical Euler buckling load of the latter when subject to axial compression. Results compare favorably with all-atom normal mode analysis, the Rotation Translation Blocks procedure, and experiment. The proposed methodology establishes a computational framework for the calculation of protein mechanical response that facilitates the incorporation of specific atomic-level interactions into the model, including aqueous-electrolyte-mediated electrostatic effects. The procedure is equally applicable to proteins with known atomic coordinates as it is to electron density maps of proteins, protein complexes, and supramolecular assemblies of unknown atomic structure.

Inspired by the elastic network model, proteins are represented as homogeneous, isotropic elastic solids whose volumes are defined by their solvent-excluded surfaces. outputs.L2: A coarse-scale computational approach using the Finite Element Method is introduced for determining the normal modes and mechanical behavior of proteins and larger supramolecular structures. Inspired by elastic network models, the method treats proteins as uniform, isotropic elastic materials whose geometry is given by the solvent-excluded molecular surface. A discretized finite-element model is created through a surface-reduction technique, allowing models to be built at any chosen spatial resolution. The approach is used to evaluate the normal modes of a T4 phage lysozyme mutant and filamentous actin, and also to determine the critical Euler buckling force for filamentous actin under axial compression. The findings agree well with all-atom normal mode calculations, the Rotation Translation Blocks method, and experimental data. outputs.L3:
A coarse-grained finite element method is proposed for calculating the normal modes and mechanical responses of proteins and supramolecular assemblies. The approach provides a continuum-based framework for studying biomolecular mechanics at length scales where fully atomistic simulations may be computationally expensive or unnecessary.

In this method, proteins are represented as homogeneous, isotropic elastic solids. Their geometries are defined by solvent-excluded molecular surfaces, which capture the overall shape of the biomolecule while smoothing over atomic-level detail. By treating the molecular volume as an elastic continuum, the method enables standard finite element techniques to be applied to biological macromolecules.

A key component of the approach is a surface simplification algorithm that allows finite element models to be generated at user-specified spatial resolutions. This makes it possible to control the level of coarse graining: finer meshes can be used when greater geometric detail is needed, while coarser meshes reduce computational cost for large assemblies. As a result, the same general procedure can be applied to individual proteins as well as much larger supramolecular structures.

The method is demonstrated through calculations of normal modes and mechanical stability properties, including Euler buckling loads. Examples such as T4 phage lysozyme and filamentous actin show that the computed results agree well with those obtained from other computational approaches and with available experimental measurements. These comparisons indicate that the finite element representation can capture the dominant low-frequency motions and large-scale mechanical behavior of biomolecular systems.

An important advantage of this framework is its flexibility. Although the basic model treats the protein as a uniform elastic body, it can be extended to include atomic-level interactions or spatial variations in material properties when such information is available. In addition, the method can be applied not only to proteins with known atomic structures but also to supramolecular assemblies described by electron density maps, even when their detailed atomic structures remain unknown. This makes the approach broadly useful for connecting structural data with mechanical function across a wide range of biological systems.
outputs.L4:
A coarse-grained Finite Element Method (FEM) procedure can be used to study the mechanical behavior and large-scale motions of proteins and supramolecular assemblies by representing them as continuous elastic bodies rather than as collections of individual atoms. In this approach, the molecular structure is converted into a homogeneous, isotropic elastic solid whose geometry is defined by its solvent-excluded surface. The resulting volume is discretized into finite elements, allowing the calculation of normal modes, deformations, and mechanical responses at a spatial resolution that can be adjusted according to the size of the system and the level of detail required.

This framework provides a practical way to analyze biomolecular motions that are often difficult to access with fully atomistic methods because of computational cost, especially for very large assemblies. By tuning the mesh resolution, the method can capture global collective motions while avoiding unnecessary atomic-level detail. At the same time, because the finite element representation is derived directly from molecular shape, it preserves the overall geometry that strongly influences mechanical behavior.

The procedure was applied to two representative biological systems: T4 phage lysozyme, a well-characterized protein often used as a benchmark for structural dynamics, and filamentous actin, a large supramolecular assembly with important mechanical functions. In both cases, the calculated normal modes and elastic responses showed good agreement with results obtained from all-atom normal mode analyses, established coarse-grained models, and available experimental observations. These comparisons indicate that the continuum elastic description is sufficient to reproduce many of the functionally relevant, low-frequency motions of proteins and assemblies.

The method therefore establishes a flexible and efficient framework for studying biomolecular mechanics across multiple length scales. It can be applied not only to high-resolution atomic structures but also to lower-resolution electron density maps, making it useful for systems whose atomic coordinates are incomplete or unavailable. In addition, the approach can be extended to include more detailed atomic-level interactions when needed, combining the efficiency of continuum modeling with the specificity of molecular structure. As a result, coarse-grained FEM offers a powerful tool for connecting molecular shape, elasticity, and biological function in proteins and large macromolecular complexes.
outputs.L5:
The Finite Element Method (FEM) is a powerful numerical technique used to solve complex engineering and mathematical problems. It is widely applied in fields such as structural analysis, heat transfer, fluid mechanics, electromagnetics, and biomechanics. The main idea of the Finite Element Method is to divide a large, complicated problem into smaller and simpler parts called finite elements.

In this method, a physical object or system is represented by a mesh made up of many small elements. These elements may be one-dimensional, two-dimensional, or three-dimensional, depending on the type of problem being studied. Each element is connected to others at specific points called nodes. By calculating the behavior of each element and combining the results, engineers and scientists can approximate the behavior of the entire system.

One of the greatest advantages of the Finite Element Method is its ability to handle complex geometries, materials, and boundary conditions. For example, FEM can be used to predict how a bridge will respond to heavy loads, how heat spreads through an engine component, or how stress is distributed in a mechanical part. This makes it an essential tool in modern design and simulation.

The process typically involves several steps. First, the geometry of the object is created. Next, the object is divided into finite elements through meshing. Then, material properties and boundary conditions are applied. After that, mathematical equations are solved for each element. Finally, the results are analyzed to understand stress, deformation, temperature, vibration, or other physical quantities.

The Finite Element Method helps reduce the need for expensive physical testing and allows engineers to improve designs before manufacturing. Because of its accuracy and flexibility, FEM has become a standard method in computer-aided engineering and scientific research. As computing power continues to increase, the Finite Element Method will remain an important tool for solving real-world problems efficiently and reliably.

counterfactuals.output:
We present a finite element–based coarse-grained framework for computing the low-frequency normal modes and mechanical response of proteins and large biomolecular assemblies. In the proposed method, an atomic structure is converted into a continuous elastic body by assigning mass and elastic properties to a volume-filling mesh derived from the molecular geometry. The resulting finite element model enables efficient solution of generalized eigenvalue problems for collective vibrational modes, as well as static deformation problems under prescribed forces or constraints. By reducing the number of degrees of freedom while retaining overall molecular shape and connectivity, the approach provides a computationally tractable alternative to all-atom normal mode analysis for systems ranging from single-domain proteins to filamentous assemblies.

We demonstrate the method on T4 lysozyme and filamentous actin (F-actin). For T4 lysozyme, the lowest-frequency modes reproduce hinge-bending and domain-opening motions consistent with established elastic network and atomistic calculations, highlighting the ability of the continuum representation to capture biologically relevant collective dynamics. For F-actin, the finite element model predicts long-wavelength bending, twisting, and stretching modes and permits direct evaluation of mechanical properties such as axial stiffness, bending rigidity, and torsional compliance. These applications illustrate that the method can bridge structural biology and continuum mechanics, allowing normal modes and force-induced conformational changes to be computed for macromolecular systems that are difficult to treat with conventional atomistic approaches.

The finite element coarse-grained formulation provides a flexible platform for incorporating heterogeneous material parameters, solvent-accessible geometry, and multiscale coupling to atomistic or experimental data. It offers a general route for analyzing protein mechanics, conformational transitions, and the elastic behavior of supramolecular assemblies with reduced computational cost while preserving the dominant collective motions relevant to biological function.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a computational biophysics study in formal journal-abstract style about modeling proteins as homogeneous isotropic elastic solids using FEM and solvent-excluded surfaces.
counterfactuals.output:
We present a computational biophysics study evaluating a continuum elastic representation of globular proteins in which molecular structures are modeled as homogeneous, isotropic elastic solids. Protein geometries were constructed from atomic coordinates using solvent-excluded molecular surfaces, thereby retaining realistic molecular shape while replacing atomistic detail with a continuous mechanical domain. Finite element meshes were generated from these surfaces and analyzed using linear elastic finite element methods to compute equilibrium deformations and low-frequency vibrational modes.

The approach was assessed by comparing predicted global mechanical responses and normal-mode characteristics with established coarse-grained and atomistic elastic network descriptions. Despite its simplified material assumptions, the continuum model reproduced major collective deformation patterns dominated by overall molecular geometry, indicating that protein shape alone can encode substantial information about low-frequency functional motions. Sensitivity analyses of elastic moduli, Poisson ratio, mesh resolution, and surface-generation parameters demonstrated that modal shapes were generally robust, whereas absolute frequencies scaled with the assigned elastic constants.

These results support the use of solvent-excluded-surface finite element modeling as an efficient framework for probing large-scale protein mechanics, particularly when qualitative deformation modes are of primary interest. The study highlights both the utility and limitations of homogeneous isotropic continuum approximations: they provide computationally tractable access to global elastic behavior but do not capture sequence-specific heterogeneity, anisotropic packing, or local atomic interactions. Overall, the findings suggest that continuum FEM models offer a complementary tool for investigating structure–mechanics relationships in proteins and for bridging molecular geometry with mesoscale biomechanical function.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical abstract for a paper that compares a coarse-grained FEM protein mechanics approach with all-atom normal mode analysis, RTB methods, and experimental results.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract** — We present a comparative assessment of a coarse-grained finite element method (FEM) for protein mechanics against established computational and experimental approaches, including all-atom normal mode analysis (NMA), rotation-translation block (RTB) normal mode methods, and available experimental observables. In the FEM representation, protein structures are converted into elastic continua using residue- or geometry-derived meshes with effective mechanical parameters, enabling low-frequency collective motions to be computed at substantially reduced computational cost relative to atomistic models. We evaluate the ability of the FEM model to reproduce global deformation patterns, mode shapes, frequency ordering, and mechanically relevant flexibility profiles across representative protein systems.

Comparisons with all-atom NMA show that the dominant low-frequency FEM modes capture the principal collective motions observed in atomistic elastic models, particularly large-scale domain bending, twisting, and hinge-like displacements. RTB calculations provide an intermediate reference, allowing separation of effects due to coarse-graining from those due to continuum mechanical approximation. Quantitative agreement is assessed using mode-overlap measures, subspace similarity, mean-square fluctuation correlations, and comparisons with experimentally inferred dynamics, including crystallographic B-factors, conformational changes between functional states, and known flexible or hinge regions. The coarse-grained FEM approach reproduces experimentally supported collective motions with accuracy comparable to RTB-based models while requiring fewer degrees of freedom and offering direct access to continuum mechanical quantities such as strain and stress distributions.

Our results indicate that FEM-based protein mechanics provides a physically interpretable and computationally efficient framework for analyzing large-scale biomolecular motions, especially for large proteins and macromolecular assemblies where all-atom NMA becomes expensive. While atomistic NMA remains superior for resolving local side-chain and residue-level fluctuations, the FEM model effectively captures the mechanically dominant modes that often govern functional conformational transitions. The comparison highlights the trade-off between resolution, computational cost, and mechanical interpretability, supporting coarse-grained FEM as a complementary tool for connecting protein structure, elasticity, and experimentally observed dynamics.

**Abstract**

Large protein assemblies often exceed the practical limits of all-atom mechanical simulation, yet their biological function is strongly influenced by collective deformation, elasticity, and shape-dependent interactions. We describe a simplified surface-based finite element approach for generating continuum mechanical models of protein structures directly from atomic coordinates or electron density maps. In this framework, molecular surfaces are extracted, smoothed, and converted into finite element meshes that preserve the overall geometry of the assembly while greatly reducing model complexity relative to atomistic descriptions. The resulting meshes can be assigned effective elastic properties and used to compute global deformation modes, stress distributions, and mechanical responses under applied constraints or loads.

The method is applicable to both well-resolved atomic structures and lower-resolution volumetric data, enabling analysis across a range of structural biology inputs. As a benchmark, T4 phage lysozyme was modeled from atomic coordinates to demonstrate that a compact globular protein can be represented by a high-quality surface-derived mesh suitable for continuum calculations. The approach was then extended to filamentous actin, illustrating its utility for large, elongated assemblies whose mechanical behavior depends on mesoscale architecture. In both examples, simplified finite element representations captured the dominant geometric features while reducing computational cost and enabling simulations that would be difficult to perform using fully atomistic models.

Surface-based finite element meshing therefore provides a practical bridge between structural biology and continuum mechanics. By transforming atomic models or electron density maps into mechanically analyzable representations, the approach supports multiscale studies of protein flexibility, assembly mechanics, and structure–function relationships in biomolecular systems.
